The core innovation lies in recasting standard APM as a Bayesian model with a structured prior. Standard APM fails in soccer due to collinearity and sparsity, where two players who always play together cannot be distinguished. The Bayesian reformulation introduces a normal prior β ~ N(0, τ²), which stabilizes estimates but still lacks discriminative power. Augmented APM improves by centering the prior on FIFA ratings, i.e., β|α ~ N(α × rating, τ²), where α is a learnable scaling factor. This allows the model to distinguish between players even when they are collinear, because their FIFA ratings differ. The key insight is that FIFA ratings act as a proxy for player quality, providing a meaningful anchor for player effect estimation. The model assumes that goal differentials are Gaussian and that player effects are additive and constant within a segment. However, the method fails when the underlying data is too coarse, such as when substituting goal differentials with expected goals. The use of time-weighted segments further refines the model by adjusting for varying segment lengths, improving robustness. In GSE, this translates to applying the same Bayesian regularization principle to NFL drives, using Madden ratings as the prior to estimate player impact in sparse, high-dimensional settings.
